4.1.1.examLens: Interpret r and r², and recognize the traps: curved relationships, outliers, and the temptation to read causation into correlation.

worked.question: For the data X = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and Y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5: (a) compute r and r². (b) Rank these by strength: r = −0.85, r = +0.60, r = 0.05, r = −0.30. (c) A team finds r = 0.92 between monthly overtime and monthly defects. Can they conclude overtime causes defects?
worked.solution:
(a) r = 6 ÷ √(10 × 6) = 0.775, and r² = 0.60.
(b) Strongest to weakest: −0.85, +0.60, −0.30, 0.05.
(c) No. A strong correlation does not show cause. Both could be driven by a third factor, such as order volume, so they should test the relationship further (Analyze tools) before acting.

4.1.2.examLens: Fit and interpret a simple regression, predict a value, complete a partly blank regression ANOVA table, and read a coefficient table.

worked.question: For X = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and Y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5: (a) Fit the line. (b) Build the ANOVA table. (c) Test the slope at α = 0.05. (d) Read the coefficient table.
worked.solution:
(a) Ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6X.
(b) SST = Σ(Y − Ȳ)² = 6. SSR = b1 × Sxy = 0.6 × 6 = 3.6. SSE = 6 − 3.6 = 2.4.

(c) The F table for df (1, 3) gives 10.13. Since 4.5 is below 10.13, fail to reject H0: slope = 0. With only 5 points, even R² = 0.60 is not enough to show a significant slope.
(d) S = √0.8 = 0.894. SE of the slope = 0.894 ÷ √10 = 0.283, so T = 0.6 ÷ 0.283 = 2.12. With df = 3, the t table shows 1.638 (0.90 column) and 2.353 (0.95 column), so the one-sided p is between 0.05 and 0.10 and the two-sided p between 0.10 and 0.20. R-sq = 60.0%. Adjusted R² = 1 − 0.4 × 4 ÷ 3 = 46.7%.

4.1.3.examLens: Look at a residual plot, say which assumption is broken, and name the fix.

worked.question: Diagnose each: (a) the residuals-versus-fits plot shows a U shape; (b) the spread of residuals widens as fitted values increase; (c) the residuals-versus-order plot shows a steady upward drift; (d) one point lies far above the others and the fitted line tilts toward it.
worked.solution: (a) Curvature: the straight-line model is wrong. Add a squared term or transform. (b) Non-constant variance (funnel): transform Y. (c) Dependence or a time effect: look at how the data were collected over time. (d) A high-leverage or influential outlier: check data integrity first, then see how much the fit changes without it.

4.1.1.a.title: Look at the scatterplot first
4.1.1.a.html: Always plot Y against X before computing anything. The picture shows whether the relationship is linear, curved, clustered, or driven by a few unusual points. A single number can hide all of that.

4.1.1.b.title: The correlation coefficient
4.1.1.b.html:
Pearson r measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship and ranges from −1 to +1. The reference sheet gives
r = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) ÷ √[ Σ(X − X̄)² × Σ(Y − Ȳ)² ].
r² is the coefficient of determination, the share of the variation in Y explained by the straight-line relationship with X.
Example (the data above): r = 6 ÷ √(10 × 6) = 6 ÷ 7.746 = 0.775, and r² = 0.60.

4.1.1.c.title: r near zero
4.1.1.c.html: r near 0 means no linear relationship. It does not mean no relationship at all. A perfect U-shaped relationship (Y = X²) can give r near 0.

4.1.1.d.title: Correlation is not causation
4.1.1.d.html: Two variables can move together because of a third (lurking) variable. Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer because of temperature, not because one causes the other. Outliers can also create or hide a correlation.

4.1.1.e.title: Spearman rank correlation
4.1.1.e.html: Extension. Spearman correlation uses the ranks of the data. It handles monotonic (always rising or always falling, not necessarily straight) and non-normal relationships.

4.1.1.f.title: Strength versus direction
4.1.1.f.html: r = −0.9 is a strong negative relationship, stronger than r = +0.6. The sign gives the direction. The distance from zero gives the strength.

4.1.1.g.title: One point, or a curve
4.1.1.g.html: One influential point far from the rest can create a high r, or destroy one. And r near 0 can hide a strong curved relationship. Look at the plot.

4.1.2.a.title: The model
4.1.2.a.html: Ŷ = b0 + b1·X (the reference sheet writes Ŷ = a + bX). Ŷ is the predicted value of Y. b0 is the intercept and b1 is the slope.

4.1.2.b.title: The least-squares estimates
4.1.2.b.html:
Slope b1 = Sxy ÷ Sxx, where Sxy = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) and Sxx = Σ(X − X̄)². Intercept b0 = Ȳ − b1·X̄.
Example (the data above): b1 = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6. b0 = 4 − 0.6 × 3 = 2.2. The equation is Ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6X.

4.1.2.c.title: Interpreting slope and intercept
4.1.2.c.html:
• Slope: the change in Y for a one-unit increase in X. Here, each extra unit of X adds about 0.6 to Y.
  • Intercept: the predicted Y when X = 0. It is often not meaningful, especially if X = 0 is outside the data.

4.1.2.d.title: R² and adjusted R²
4.1.2.d.html: R² is the share of the variation in Y explained by the model. Adjusted R² corrects for the number of terms, so adding a useless predictor does not inflate it. For one predictor, R² equals r².

4.1.2.e.title: S and the slope test
4.1.2.e.html: S is the standard error of the regression: the typical distance of the data from the line, in the units of Y. S = √(SSE ÷ (n − 2)). The p-value for the slope tests H0: slope = 0 (no linear relationship).

4.1.2.f.title: The regression ANOVA table
4.1.2.f.html: It splits the total variation: SST = SSR + SSE. SSR is explained by the line, SSE is the leftover (residual) variation, and F tests whether the model explains more than chance.

4.1.2.g.title: Do not extrapolate
4.1.2.g.html: The line is only known to hold within the range of the data. Predicting outside that range (extrapolation) assumes the relationship continues, which may not be true.

4.1.2.h.title: Predicting Ŷ
4.1.2.h.html:
Plug X into the equation.
Example: X = 3.5 gives Ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6 × 3.5 = 4.3. X = 6 is outside the data (1 to 5), so a prediction there is extrapolation and should not be trusted.

4.1.2.i.title: What R² = 0.72 means
4.1.2.i.html: 72% of the variation in Y is explained by the model. The sign of r comes from the slope (a negative slope gives a negative r). R² itself is always positive.

4.1.2.j.title: Regression ANOVA, degrees of freedom
4.1.2.j.html:
• Simple regression: df = 1 (regression), n − 2 (error), n − 1 (total).
  • Multiple regression with k predictors: df = k, n − k − 1, n − 1.
  • F = MS regression ÷ MS error, with MS = SS ÷ df.
  • R² = SS regression ÷ SS total.

Exams often give a partially blank table and ask you to fill it in.
Example: n = 12, SST = 50, SSE = 20 (simple regression). SSR = 30. df = 1, 10, 11. MSR = 30, MSE = 2. F = 15. The F table for df (1, 10) gives 4.96, so the regression is significant. R² = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.60.

4.1.2.k.title: The slope's confidence interval
4.1.2.k.html: If the confidence interval for the slope contains 0, you fail to reject H0: slope = 0 at the matching α. If it excludes 0, the relationship is significant.

4.1.2.l.title: Reading a coefficient table
4.1.2.l.html: Columns: Coef (the estimate), SE Coef (its standard error), T (Coef ÷ SE Coef), P (the p-value). Below the table, S, R-sq, R-sq(adj), and R-sq(pred) (how well the model predicts new data).

4.1.2.m.title: What the reference sheet does and does not give
4.1.2.m.html:
The sheet gives r, Ŷ = a + bX, the multiple regression equation, and the multiple standard error SE = √[ Σ(Y − Ŷ)² ÷ (n − (k + 1)) ].
Not on the sheet: the slope and intercept formulas, R², adjusted R², F, VIF, and the interval formulas. Know them, or expect software output.

4.1.3.a.title: The residual
4.1.3.a.html:
e = y − ŷ, the observed value minus the fitted value. The residuals from a least-squares line add up to zero.
Example (the data above): Ŷ = 2.8, 3.4, 4.0, 4.6, 5.2 for X = 1 to 5. Residuals = 2 − 2.8, 4 − 3.4, 5 − 4.0, 4 − 4.6, 5 − 5.2 = −0.8, 0.6, 1.0, −0.6, −0.2. Sum = 0. Sum of squares = 2.4 = SSE.

4.1.3.b.title: The model assumptions
4.1.3.b.html:
• The relationship is linear (a straight line is the right shape).
  • Errors are independent.
  • Errors have constant variance.
  • Errors are approximately normal.

The residuals should be centered near zero.

4.1.3.c.title: Normal probability plot of the residuals
4.1.3.c.html: Checks the normality of the errors. Points near a straight line mean approximately normal.

4.1.3.d.title: Residuals versus fitted values
4.1.3.d.html:
• Random scatter with no pattern: good.
  • A funnel (spread grows or shrinks): non-constant variance.
  • A curve: the relationship is not linear and the model needs another term.

4.1.3.e.title: Residuals versus order
4.1.3.e.html: Plot the residuals in the order the data were collected. A pattern (trend, cycles, runs) signals dependence between observations or a time effect.

4.1.3.f.title: Outliers, leverage, and influence
4.1.3.f.html:
• An outlier has a large residual (far from the line in Y).
  • High leverage means an X value far from the other X values.
  • An influential point changes the fitted line substantially if removed.

4.1.3.g.title: Diagnose and fix
4.1.3.g.html: Given a residual plot, name the violation and the fix (transform the data, or add a term).

4.1.3.h.title: Diagnostic to action
4.1.3.h.html:
• Curve in residuals versus fits: wrong functional form. Add a term (for example X²) or transform.
  • Funnel: non-constant variance. Transform Y.
  • Pattern versus order: dependence or time effect. Investigate how the data were collected.
  • One extreme point: check influence and data integrity (is it a recording error?).

4.1.1-1.stem: Which correlation coefficient shows the strongest linear relationship?
4.1.1-1.explanation: Strength is the distance from zero. The sign gives only the direction.

4.1.1-2.stem: A scatterplot shows a correlation of r = −0.8. What is the coefficient of determination, and what does it mean?

options.html: 0.64; 64% of the variation in Y is explained by the linear relationship with X

4.1.1-2.explanation: r² = 0.64, so 64% of the variation in Y is explained by the straight-line relationship with X.

4.1.1-3.stem: If r is close to 0, there is no relationship of any kind between X and Y.
4.1.1-3.explanation: r measures only linear relationships. A strong curved relationship, such as a U shape, can have r near 0.

4.1.1-4.stem: A team finds r = 0.92 between monthly overtime hours and monthly defects. Can they conclude that overtime causes defects?

options.html: Yes, because r is very high
No; both could be driven by a third factor, such as order volume, so the relationship needs further testing
Yes, because the relationship is linear
No, because correlation can only be negative

4.1.1-4.explanation: Correlation is not causation. A lurking variable or one influential point can create a strong correlation.

4.1.2-1.stem: A fitted line is Ŷ = 3 + 2X. What is the predicted value at X = 4?

4.1.2-2.stem: A regression of test score (Y) on hours of training (X) gives Ŷ = 20 + 1.5X. What does the slope mean?

options.html: Each extra hour of training adds about 1.5 points to the predicted score
Each point of score adds 1.5 hours

4.1.2-2.explanation: The slope is the change in Y for a one-unit change in X.

4.1.2-3.stem: A simple regression with n = 11 has SST = 100 and SSE = 36. The α = 0.05 critical F for df (1, 9) is 5.12. What are F and R², and is the regression significant?
4.1.2-3.explanation: SSR = 100 − 36 = 64 (df 1). SSE has df = n − 2 = 9. MSR = 64 and MSE = 4, so F = 16, which exceeds 5.12. R² = 64 ÷ 100 = 0.64.

4.1.2-4.stem: The 95% confidence interval for a regression slope is −0.2 to 1.4. What does this indicate?

options.html: The slope is significant, because the interval is wide
The slope is not significantly different from zero at α = 0.05, because the interval contains zero
The model has a perfect fit

4.1.2-4.explanation: An interval containing zero corresponds to failing to reject H0: slope = 0.

4.1.2-5.stem: A line was fitted using temperatures from 150 to 220 °C. A manager asks for a prediction at 280 °C. What is the best response?

options.html: Plug 280 into the equation and report the result
Decline to rely on it, because 280 °C is outside the data range and the relationship may not hold there
Report the result with a wider confidence interval
Use the intercept as the prediction

4.1.2-5.explanation: Predicting outside the range of the data is extrapolation and should not be trusted.

4.1.2-6.stem: A model with R² = 0.72 explains 72% of the variation in Y.
4.1.2-6.explanation: R² is the share of the variation in Y explained by the model.

4.1.2-7.stem: In a coefficient table, the slope is 0.6 with a standard error of 0.3, and df = 8 (critical t = 2.306 at α = 0.05, two-sided). What is the decision on H0: slope = 0?

options.html: Reject H0, since t = 2.0 is near 2.3
Fail to reject H0, since t = 2.0 is below 2.306
Fail to reject H0, since t = 20

4.1.2-7.explanation: t = Coef ÷ SE Coef = 0.6 ÷ 0.3 = 2.0, which is below 2.306.

4.1.3-1.stem: An observed value is 12 and the fitted value is 10.4. What is the residual?

4.1.3-2.stem: A plot of residuals versus fitted values shows the spread of the residuals widening as the fitted values increase. Which assumption is violated, and what is a reasonable fix?
4.1.3-2.explanation: A funnel shape means non-constant variance. A transformation such as a log or Box-Cox often helps.

4.1.3-3.stem: A plot of residuals versus fitted values shows a clear U shape. What does this indicate?

options.html: The straight-line model is wrong; add a squared term or transform

4.1.3-3.explanation: A curve in the residuals means the functional form is wrong.

4.1.3-4.stem: A plot of residuals in the order the data were collected shows a steady upward drift. What does this suggest?

options.html: A dependence between observations or a time effect

4.1.3-4.explanation: Patterns versus order indicate dependence or a time effect, such as instrument drift or learning.

4.1.3-5.stem: One data point lies far from the others and the fitted line tilts toward it. What should be done first?

options.html: Check the data point for a recording error, then see how much the fit changes without it

4.1.3-5.explanation: Check data integrity first, then assess whether the point is influential.

4.1.3-6.stem: Which TWO are assumptions behind the usual inference in simple regression?
4.1.3-6.explanation: The model assumes a linear mean, independent errors with constant variance, and approximately normal errors. X need not be normal and the slope may be any sign.

4.1.2-11.text: A regression with n = 12 has a slope coefficient of 1.5 and a standard error of 0.5. Test H0: slope = 0 at α = 0.05 (two-sided).
4.1.2-11.answer: t = 1.5 ÷ 0.5 = 3.00, df = 10. Critical = 2.228. Reject H0: the slope is significant.

4.1.2-13.text: A regression with n = 8 has a slope coefficient of 2.0 and a standard error of 1.2. Test H0: slope = 0 at α = 0.05 (two-sided).

4.1.2-14.text: A regression with n = 20 has a slope coefficient of 2.0 and a standard error of 0.8. Test H0: slope = 0 at α = 0.05 (two-sided).
